qs.q: Which drug targets the vicynyl sulfhydryl groups of pyruvate kinase? ---
qs.e: Melarsoprol binds to vicinal sulfhydryl groups of parasite enzymes like pyruvate kinase.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an inherited enzyme defect causing chronic hemolytic anemia. Red cells lack ATP, leading to membrane rigidity, premature destruction, and compensatory 2,3‑DPG rise.

sections.p: A hereditary loss‑of‑function mutation in the PKLR gene reduces red‑cell pyruvate kinase activity, impairing glycolysis and ATP generation.
b: Diagnosis requires low PK enzyme activity in RBCs (<10% of normal) plus genetic confirmation.
Exclude other hemolytic causes with Coombs test, G6PD assay, and osmotic fragility.

t.b: Does the patient have reduced PK activity? Low activity confirms the defect.
Is a pathogenic mutation present? Identifies carrier status and guides counseling.
Is there anemia with reticulocytosis? Shows chronic hemolysis.

sections.p: Severity is graded by transfusion dependence and hemoglobin level.
b: Mild: Hb ≥ 10 g/dL, no regular transfusions.
Moderate: Hb 8‑10 g/dL, occasional transfusions.
Severe: Hb < 8 g/dL, chronic transfusion requirement.

sections.p: PK deficiency is autosomal recessive; other hemolytic disorders can coexist.
b: PKLR gene mutation (most common cause).
Co‑existing hereditary spherocytosis or thalassemia (common in low‑resource settings).
Infections that increase hemolysis (malaria, sepsis).

sections.p: Patients develop lifelong anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and gallstones; neonates may have severe hyperbilirubinemia.
b: Fatigue, pallor, and exertional dyspnea.
Pigmented gallstones from chronic bilirubin overload.
Growth retardation in severe cases.

sections.p: Laboratory work‑up confirms hemolysis and identifies the enzyme defect.
b: Peripheral smear shows echinocytes and occasional spherocytes.
Elevated LDH, indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin.

t.b: What cell morphology is present? Echinocytes suggest PK deficiency.
Is hemolysis ongoing? High indirect bilirubin/LDH, low haptoglobin confirm.
Are gallstones present? Detects pigment stones common in chronic hemolysis.

sections.p: Complications arise from severe anemia and chronic hemolysis.
b: Acute aplastic crisis (often triggered by parvovirus B19).
Severe hyperbilirubinemia leading to kernicterus in neonates.
Iron overload from repeated transfusions.

sections.p: Treat the hemolysis, prevent complications, and support quality of life.
b: Folic acid supplementation to support erythropoiesis.
Transfusion for severe anemia; avoid over‑transfusion to limit iron overload.
Splenectomy in transfusion‑dependent patients improves hemoglobin.
Consider experimental gene therapy where available.
Quarterly CBC and reticulocyte count.
Annual liver iron assessment (MRI or ferritin) if transfused.
Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms before splenectomy.

sections.p: Other chronic hemolytic anemias share similar signs.
b: Hereditary spherocytosis – membrane protein defect, positive osmotic fragility test.
G6PD deficiency – episodic hemolysis after oxidative stress.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia – positive Coombs test.

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite disease.
b: PK activity can be falsely normal if sample is hemolyzed; repeat assay.
Reticulocyte count may be low during aplastic crisis, masking chronic hemolysis.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening anemia with fatigue, tachycardia, or chest pain.
Acute jaundice with dark urine in a newborn.
Fever and rapid drop in hemoglobin suggesting aplastic crisis.

faq.q: Why does PK deficiency cause increased 2,3‑DPG?
faq.a: Low ATP forces red cells to shift glycolysis, accumulating 2,3‑DPG which lowers oxygen affinity and partially compensates for anemia.
It improves hemoglobin by reducing destruction but does not correct the enzyme defect; lifelong monitoring remains essential.
Heterozygotes usually have normal PK activity and are asymptomatic, though mild anemia can occur under stress.

exam: Describe the pathophysiology of hemolysis in pyruvate kinase deficiency.

Explain the indications, benefits, and risks of splenectomy in PK deficiency.
